summary: Surveys use of IPv4 addresses in IETF Routing Area standards-track and experimental documents, to find dependencies on IPv4 as a step towards IPv6. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A checklist of routing rules that mention old-style addresses, so they can be updated.

questions: ipv4 dependencies in routing area specs
do bgp ospf and rip support ipv6
how does bgp carry ipv6 routes
subtitle: Comprehensive survey of IPv4 dependencies in routing protocols like BGP, OSPF, and RIP.

tldr.problem: Routing protocols are fundamental to Internet operation, but nearly all were designed for IPv4. BGP, OSPF, RIP, and dozens of other routing protocols assume 32-bit IPv4 addresses are the standard.
tldr.mechanism: This survey examines 46 Routing Area RFCs (Full, Draft, Proposed Standards, and Experimental) to catalog IPv4 dependencies in routing protocols and identify what changes would be needed for IPv6 routing.
tldr.outcome: The Routing Area had the highest percentage of IPv4 dependencies (23 out of 46, or 50%) of any IETF area surveyed. However, IPv6 versions of major protocols (OSPFv3, RIPng, multiprotocol BGP) were already being developed.

today: RFC 3791 remains informational. It documented the state of routing protocols in 2004 and guided protocol designers toward IPv6-capable routing. Major routing protocols have since been updated or supplemented: multiprotocol BGP (RFC 2858) enables BGP-4 to carry IPv6 routes, OSPFv3 and RIPng provide native IPv6 routing within networks, and modern routers support both IPv4 and IPv6 routing simultaneously.

sections.title: Why Routing Protocols Matter for IPv6
sections.content:
Routing protocols determine how data packets find their way across the Internet from source to destination. Unlike application-layer protocols that individual programs use, routing protocols are fundamental to the Internet's infrastructure. Every router—from small campus networks to global backbone carriers—uses routing protocols to exchange information about which networks are reachable and the best path to reach them.

The three major classes of routing protocols each handle IPv4 differently. Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) like OSPF and RIP manage routing within an autonomous system (a group of networks under single administration). Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) manages routing between autonomous systems and is critical for the global Internet's interconnection. Multicast routing adds another dimension. All of these must function during the IPv4-to-IPv6 transition.
sections.eli5: Routers are computers that decide where to send information next. They use special rules to figure out the best path. Almost every one of these rules was written for old addresses only.

sections.title: Full Standards: The Core Routing Protocols
sections.content:
All 3 Full Standards in the Routing Area have IPv4 dependencies. These are the most critical routing protocols in the Internet:

RFC 2328 (OSPF Version 2) is the most widely deployed interior gateway protocol for large networks. Its specification is highly assumptive about IPv4 address formats. It encodes IPv4 network addresses in its link-state advertisements and uses IPv4 multicast addresses (224.0.0.5 and 224.0.0.6) for protocol communication.

RFC 2453 (RIP Version 2) and RFC 1722 (RIP Version 2 Applicability Statement) define RIP, an older but still widely used interior gateway protocol. Both RFCs explicitly state that RIPv2 is intended only for IPv4 networks.

The existence of IPv6 versions (OSPFv3 and RIPng) in the standards process acknowledged that entirely new protocols rather than simple extensions were sometimes necessary.
sections.eli5: The main rules for routing inside a company's network all only work with old addresses. RIP is older and simpler. OSPF is newer and handles bigger networks. Both need completely new versions for new addresses.

sections.title: Draft Standards: BGP and Its Extensions
sections.content:
Among 3 Draft Standards in the Routing Area, 1 (33.3%) has IPv4 dependencies: RFC 1771 (Border Gateway Protocol 4). BGP-4 is the protocol that holds the global Internet together, exchanging routing information between backbone networks and autonomous systems. The RFC explicitly states that it does not support IPv6 as currently defined.

However, RFC 3392 (BGP-4 Capabilities Advertisement) extends BGP but notes that while the extensions themselves are not IPv4-specific, the base protocol remains IPv4-only. This points to a solution: RFC 2858, which adds multiprotocol extensions to BGP-4, allows BGP to carry routing information for multiple network layer protocols including IPv6. This extension, developed during the survey period, became critical for the transition.
sections.eli5: BGP is the super-important rule that tells the whole Internet how to get to every network. It only works with old addresses, but there are plans to make it flexible enough for both kinds.

sections.title: Proposed Standards: CIDR, Variants, and Alternatives
sections.content:
Among 29 Proposed Standards in the Routing Area, 13 (44.8%) have IPv4 dependencies. These include:

CIDR standards: RFC 1517, 1518, and 1519 document Classless Inter-Domain Routing, which deals exclusively with IPv4 address allocation and aggregation strategies. CIDR was crucial for extending IPv4's life but is not directly applicable to IPv6's design.

Routing extensions: RFC 1195 (IS-IS for TCP/IP) extends IS-IS routing to IPv4. RFC 1584 (Multicast Extensions to OSPF) adds IPv4 multicast routing. RFC 2784 (Generic Routing Encapsulation) is defined only for IPv4 in its original form, though the document acknowledges IPv6 as a potential future extension.

Protocols designed for dual-stack or IPv6: RFC 2891 (RIPng for IPv6), RFC 2740 (OSPF for IPv6), RFC 2858 (Multiprotocol Extensions for BGP-4), and RFC 2894 (Router Renumbering for IPv6) are IPv6-specific or explicitly support multiple protocols and are not further examined in this survey's context.
sections.eli5: Some of the proposed rules for better ways to organize and distribute routing information only work with old addresses. Others are already designed for new addresses. A few can work with both.

sections.title: Experimental Protocols and Multicast Routing
sections.content:
Among 11 Experimental RFCs in the Routing Area, 6 (54.5%) have IPv4 dependencies. These include multicast routing protocols which add complexity: RFC 1075 (Distance Vector Multicast Routing Protocol) defines IPv4 multicast routing. RFC 1383 (DNS Based IP Routing) proposes IPv4-specific routing extensions using DNS. Various others explore alternative approaches.

Multicast routing (routing to multiple destinations simultaneously) is one of the most IPv4-specific aspects of routing. IPv4 reserves address ranges 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 for multicast. Protocols like DVMRP, Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM), and Multicast Source Discovery Protocol (MSDP) all assume IPv4 multicast addresses. Adapting multicast routing for IPv6, which has a different multicast architecture, required significant redesign.
sections.eli5: Some experimental rules try different ways to send information to many computers at once. This is complicated with old addresses and needed new ideas for new addresses.
